1	# Data Lineage Trust Platform
2	
3	Backend service for managing datasets, their immutable schema versions and
4	field-level lineage between schema versions. All metadata is persisted in a
5	SQLite database, so data created before a restart remains queryable afterwards.
6	
7	## Requirements
8	
9	- Python 3.12+
10	
11	## Install and test
12	
13	```bash
14	python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
15	python -m pytest
16	```
17	
18	## Start
19	
20	```bash
21	python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
22	```
23	
24	The SQLite database is stored at `data/lineage.db` by default. Override the
25	location with the `DATA_LINEAGE_DB` environment variable.
26	
27	## Public API
28	
29	All endpoints return JSON. Error responses use the stable shape
30	`{"error": "<code>", "detail": "<message>"}` and never expose SQL or stack
31	traces.
32	
33	### Health
34	
35	- `GET /health` returns `{"status":"ok"}` when the service is ready.
36	
37	### Datasets
38	
39	- `POST /datasets` — create a dataset. Body: `{"name": "orders", "description": "optional"}`.
40	  Returns `201` with `id`, `name`, `description`, `created_at`. Empty name →
41	  `422`; duplicate name → `409`.
42	- `GET /datasets` — list all datasets.
43	
44	### Schema versions (immutable, numbered from 1 per dataset)
45	
46	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — create the next schema version. Body:
47	  `{"fields": [{"name": "id", "type": "integer", "nullable": false}]}`.
48	  Field list must be non-empty, field `name`/`type`/`nullable` are required and
49	  field names must be unique within the version. Unknown dataset → `404`;
50	  invalid fields → `422` (nothing is written).
51	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — list all versions of a dataset with
52	  their fields.
53	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}` — read one version with its
54	  fields. Unknown dataset/version → `404`.
55	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}` —
56	  read-only breaking-change check of the target version against the base
57	  version, computed fresh from the persisted field definitions on every read
58	  (nothing is written; field order is not a difference). The endpoint takes no
59	  request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version →
60	  `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the version diff. The JSON
61	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
62	  trailing newline) with top-level keys `base_version`, `target_version`,
63	  `breaking_changes` and `breaking_change_count`. A breaking change is exactly
64	  one of: the target removed a base field (`removed`), changed a field's type
65	  (`type_changed`) or tightened a nullable field to not nullable
66	  (`nullable_tightened`); added fields and nullable loosening are not
67	  breaking. Each entry has `field`, `kind`, `before` (base definition) and
68	  `after` (target definition, `null` for a removed field), entries are sorted
69	  by field name ascending and `breaking_change_count` equals the number of
70	  entries. Comparing a version with itself returns an empty list and a zero
71	  count. The verdict is advisory for release decisions only: it runs no
72	  migration or rollback.
73	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}/impact` —
74	  read-only companion of the compatibility check: the same top-level keys
75	  (`base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_changes`,
76	  `breaking_change_count`) and the same breaking entries, each entry carrying
77	  one extra key `impacted` after `after`. `impacted` lists every field
78	  directly or indirectly downstream of the broken field along the lineage
79	  mappings, starting from the base version's same-named field and — when the
80	  field still exists in the target version — also from the target version's
81	  field. Each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`; the set is
82	  deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate) and is
83	  sorted by dataset, version and field ascending. A field with no downstream
84	  yields an empty list. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
85	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404` with the same
86	  404-before-422 precedence as the compatibility check, and the JSON document
87	  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
88	  newline). The read is fully side-effect free: version definitions, lineage
89	  mappings and the impact cache are never written.
90	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/evolution-summary` — read-only whole-dataset
91	  summary of adjacent-version breaking changes and their downstream impact,
92	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version
93	  definitions, lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched).
94	  Quality and privacy state play no role. The path carries only the dataset
95	  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an unknown
96	  dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
97	  compatibility reads. A dataset with fewer than two versions returns `200`
98	  with an empty `pairs` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
99	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
100	  trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`, `pairs` and `totals`.
101	  `pairs` is ordered by base version number ascending and lists every
102	  adjacent version pair, including pairs without breaking changes; each entry
103	  has exactly `base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_count`,
104	  `impacted_count` and `impacted_datasets` in that order. `breaking_count` is
105	  the number of breaking entries of the pair, judged exactly as in the
106	  pairwise compatibility impact response (`removed`, `type_changed` or
107	  `nullable_tightened`; several changes of one field collapse into a single
108	  entry). The pair's impacted set is the union of every breaking entry's
109	  downstream fields — same start-field rule as the pairwise impact response,
110	  merged and deduplicated, never containing a start field itself (cycles
111	  terminate) — `impacted_count` is its size and `impacted_datasets` lists the
112	  distinct dataset names appearing in it, sorted ascending. `totals` has
113	  exactly `pair_count` (the number of pairs), `breaking_count` and
114	  `impacted_count`, each the sum of the per-pair values over the whole
115	  dataset.
116	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/fields/{field}/trajectory` — read-only
117	  cross-version trajectory of one named field of the dataset, computed fresh
118	  on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions,
119	  lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched). Only the
120	  persisted version field definitions and lineage mappings are read; quality,
121	  privacy, snapshot and processing-task state play no role. The path carries
122	  the dataset name and the field name; the request takes no body and no query
123	  parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, and a field that does not
124	  appear in any of the dataset's versions → `404`, both with the same
125	  404-before-422 precedence as the evolution summary. A dataset with fewer
126	  than two versions returns `200` with an empty `changes` array, never an
127	  error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
128	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
129	  `field`, `entries` and `changes` in that order. `entries` lists every
130	  schema version of the dataset ordered by version number ascending; each
131	  entry has exactly `version` and `definition`, where `definition` is the
132	  field's persisted definition in that version (`type` and `nullable` only)
133	  or `null` — the key is never omitted — when the field does not exist
134	  there. `changes` lists one entry per adjacent version pair, ordered by
135	  base version ascending; each entry has exactly `base_version`,
136	  `target_version`, `status`, `impacted` and `impacted_datasets` in that
137	  order. `status` reuses the breaking-entry vocabulary of the compatibility
138	  check — `added` (the field appears on the target side), `removed` (it
139	  disappears on the target side), `type_changed`, `nullable_tightened` —
140	  extended with `nullable_loosened` (only the nullability relaxes) and
141	  `unchanged` (both definitions agree, including both absent); a field that
142	  both changes type and tightens nullability collapses into a single
143	  `type_changed` status. `impacted` lists every field directly or indirectly
144	  downstream of the tracked field for that pair along the lineage mappings,
145	  with the same start-field rule as the pairwise compatibility impact
146	  response (the base version's same-named field and, when it exists, the
147	  target version's); each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`, the set
148	  is deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate),
149	  is sorted by dataset, version and field ascending and is empty when the
150	  field has no downstream. `impacted_datasets` lists the distinct dataset
151	  names appearing in `impacted`, sorted ascending.
152	
153	### Field-level lineage
154	
155	A lineage link maps one field of a target schema version to one field of a
156	schema version in a different (source) dataset.
157	
158	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — register a mapping.
159	  Body names both ends:
160	
161	  ```json
162	  {
163	    "target_dataset": "dm_orders",
164	    "target_version": 1,
165	    "target_field": "id",
166	    "source_dataset": "raw_orders",
167	    "source_version": 1,
168	    "source_field": "order_id"
169	  }
170	  ```
171	
172	  Target must match the path. Source and target datasets must differ and every
173	  referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404` / `422` otherwise).
174	  Submitting the same complete mapping twice returns `409`.
175	- `DELETE /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — remove one
176	  registered mapping. Same address and same body shape as registration: the
177	  six locating fields name the complete mapping to delete and the body target
178	  must match the path. Every locating value readable in the request is
179	  resolved first, so an unknown dataset, version or field is a `404` ahead of
180	  every request-shape error; when all six values name existing resources but
181	  the mapping itself was never registered, the delete is likewise a `404`.
182	  An empty or whitespace body, invalid JSON, a non-object payload, missing or
183	  extra fields, wrongly typed values, blank names, any query parameter, a
184	  mapping whose source and target datasets coincide or whose body target
185	  disagrees with the path are all `422`. No rejection changes the lineage
186	  graph, the impact cache or any other metadata. A registered mapping is
187	  deleted atomically and returns `200` with the removed mapping in the
188	  registration response shape; concurrent deletes of the same mapping succeed
189	  exactly once (the loser gets `404` and changes nothing). The deletion is
190	  visible to every lineage read immediately and survives restarts; the cached
191	  impacts of the mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it
192	  are invalidated exactly as on registration, unrelated entries are kept.
193	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — return every target
194	  field (including fields without sources) together with its source references.
195	  Results are sorted by target field name, then source dataset name, source
196	  version and source field name.
197	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact?field=<field>` —
198	  return the downstream impact of one source field. The path and the `field`
199	  query parameter together name an existing field; the response is
200	  `{"source": {...}, "impacted": [...]}` where `impacted` lists every field
201	  reachable from the source along lineage mappings (direct and indirect), each
202	  entry being `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. Results are deduplicated,
203	  never contain the source itself (cycles terminate) and are sorted by dataset,
204	  version and field ascending. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; a
205	  missing, blank, invalid or repeated `field` parameter → `422` (a repeated
206	  `field` is judged before the field lookup, so it is always a `422`, never a
207	  field `404`).
208	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit` —
209	  read-only consistency audit of the version's impact cache, appended one
210	  segment after the impact query address. The path dataset and version name
211	  the audit scope; every field of that version is checked against its current
212	  cache record and recomputed fresh from the committed lineage graph using
213	  exactly the impact-query semantics (downstream fields merged and
214	  deduplicated, the start field excluded, cycles terminating). Each entry is
215	  `{"field", "status"}` with `cached` (the stored record equals the
216	  recomputed result), `missing` (no cache record because the field's impact
217	  was never queried — a normal state, not an error) or `mismatch` (the stored
218	  record differs). Entries are sorted by field name ascending and the sort
219	  does not depend on database order. The JSON document is deterministic
220	  (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with
221	  top-level keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order;
222	  `counts` gives `cached_count`, `missing_count` and `mismatch_count`, each
223	  equal to the number of entries with that status. The audit is computed on
224	  every read and never writes: no cache record is inserted, invalidated or
225	  repaired, so impact queries, impact paths and source paths behave exactly
226	  as before. The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters; any
227	  body bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, and an
228	  unknown dataset or version → `404`, with `404` taking precedence over
229	  `422` as in the impact query.
230	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit/repair`
231	  — controlled repair of the version's impact cache, appended one segment
232	  after the read-only audit address and accepting POST only. Every field of
233	  the version is recomputed against the committed lineage graph with the
234	  exact impact-query semantics: a field without a cache record gets one
235	  (`created`), a stored record that disagrees is rewritten (`updated`) and a
236	  matching record is left untouched (`unchanged`). Entries are sorted by
237	  field name ascending and the JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
238	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level
239	  keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order; each
240	  entry has exactly `field` and `action`, and `counts` gives
241	  `created_count`, `updated_count` and `unchanged_count`. Written records
242	  are ordinary cache rows visible immediately to impact queries and
243	  surviving restarts; a subsequent audit reports every field as `cached`.
244	  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters — any body
245	  bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, an unknown
246	  dataset or version → `404` (with `404` taking precedence as in the audit),
247	  and concurrent repairs of the same version have a single winner, the
248	  loser receiving `409` and changing nothing. Every rejection writes
249	  nothing; lineage registrations and deletions, impact queries, path
250	  explanations, source-path reads and the read-only audit are unaffected.
251	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-invalidations`
252	  — read-only invalidation trail of the version's impact cache, appended one
253	  segment after the impact query address and accepting GET only. Whenever a
254	  lineage mapping is successfully registered or deleted, every invalidated
255	  field that actually had a cache record (the mapping's source field and
256	  every field that can reach it) leaves one append-only record under its own
257	  dataset and version; cache invalidation triggered by schema version
258	  creation leaves no trail. Each entry has exactly `sequence`, `cause`,
259	  `field` and `created_at` in that order: `sequence` numbers the version's
260	  records from 1 in write order (continuous, never reused, even under
261	  concurrent registrations and deletions), `cause` is `registered` or
262	  `deleted` after the triggering mapping write and `created_at` is the
263	  timezone-bearing write time. Entries are sorted by sequence ascending and
264	  a version without records returns an empty `entries` array, never an
265	  error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
266	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
267	  `version` and `entries` in that order. The trail is append-only and
268	  survives restarts; the read only reads persisted records and never writes,
269	  invalidates or repairs anything. The endpoint takes no request body and no
270	  query parameters; any body bytes (whitespace-only included) or query
271	  parameter → `422`, and an unknown dataset or version → `404`, with `404`
272	  taking precedence over `422` as in the impact query.
273	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact-paths?field=<field>` —
274	  read-only shortest-path explanation of the same impact, computed fresh on
275	  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
276	  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
277	  query parameter together name an existing field. The JSON document is
278	  deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
279	  newline) with top-level keys `source`, `impacts`, `direct_count` and
280	  `indirect_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
281	  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `impacts` entry has exactly the
282	  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
283	  entries are deduplicated, never contain the source and are sorted by dataset,
284	  version and field ascending. `path` is the shortest node sequence from the
285	  source to the field, including both ends, and each node has the same
286	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
287	  edges on the path (`1` for a direct downstream field, increasing for
288	  indirect ones). Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest
289	  node sequence (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles
290	  terminate. `direct_count` counts fields at distance 1 and `indirect_count`
291	  the fields farther away, and a field with no downstream returns an empty
292	  `impacts` array and both counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no
293	  request body and no query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or
294	  repeated `field` is likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field →
295	  `404`, with `404` taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated
296	  `field` is judged before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.
297	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/source-paths?field=<field>` —
298	  read-only upstream companion of the lineage impact query, computed fresh on
299	  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
300	  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
301	  query parameter together name an existing field; the `field` value is
302	  matched literally (never trimmed), so a whitespace-padded name that matches
303	  no stored field is a `404`. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
304	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys
305	  `source`, `origins`, `direct_count`, `indirect_count` and
306	  `source_dataset_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
307	  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `origins` entry has exactly the
308	  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
309	  entries are deduplicated, never contain the start field and are sorted by
310	  dataset, version and field ascending. An origin is a field whose mapping
311	  points (directly or transitively) at the start field. `path` is the
312	  shortest node sequence walking from the start field up to the origin,
313	  including both ends, and each node has the same
314	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
315	  edges on the path (`1` for a direct source, increasing for indirect ones).
316	  Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest node sequence
317	  (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles terminate.
318	  `direct_count` counts origins at distance 1, `indirect_count` the origins
319	  farther away and `source_dataset_count` the distinct dataset names among
320	  all origins; a field with no sources returns an empty `origins` array and
321	  all counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no request body and no
322	  query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or repeated `field` is
323	  likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field → `404`, with `404`
324	  taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated `field` is judged
325	  before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.
326	
327	  Impact results are cached persistently (they survive restarts) and every
328	  read reflects the currently committed lineage graph: creating a schema
329	  version invalidates the cache entries related to that dataset, and creating
330	  or deleting a lineage mapping invalidates the cached impacts of the
331	  mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it. Unrelated
332	  cache entries are preserved.
333	
334	### Quality rules
335	
336	Quality rules validate rows against a schema version. Rules are version-scoped
337	and persisted (including their enabled state) across restarts.
338	
339	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — create a rule.
340	  Body: `{"name": "id required", "kind": "not_null", "params": {...}}`. Returns
341	  `201` with `id`, `name`, `kind`, `params`, `enabled`, `created_at`; `enabled`
342	  defaults to `true`. Rule names must be unique within a version (`409` on
343	  conflict). Referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404`); other invalid
344	  input returns `422` and nothing is written. Supported kinds:
345	  - `not_null` — params `{"field": "<existing field>"}`.
346	  - `numeric_range` — params `{"field": "<existing field>", "min": <finite
347	    number>, "max": <finite number>}` with `min <= max`.
348	  - `unique` — params `{"fields": ["<existing field>", ...]}`: a non-empty list
349	    of distinct, existing field names.
350	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — list rules
351	  sorted by `id` ascending.
352	- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/{rule_id}` —
353	  enable or disable a rule. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
354	  the updated rule. Unknown rule/dataset/version → `404`.
355	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluate` —
356	  evaluate rows. Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}`. Only enabled rules run.
357	  Returns `{"dataset", "version", "results"}` with results sorted by `rule_id`;
358	  each result has `rule_id`, `name`, `passed` and `violations` (0-based row
359	  indices in ascending order).
360	  - `not_null` fails on missing or `null` values.
361	  - `numeric_range` fails on missing, `null`, non-numeric, boolean or
362	    out-of-range values (boundaries included).
363	  - `unique` compares the tuple of `fields` values per row; a missing field
364	    counts as `null`, and every row taking part in a duplicate group is a
365	    violation.
366	  - With an empty `rows` list every rule passes.
367	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations` —
368	  list the persisted evaluation history of the version, ordered by `sequence`
369	  (occurrence order). Every successful evaluation appends one immutable
370	  summary (`sequence`, `dataset`, `version`, `row_count`,
371	  `violation_row_count` — the number of distinct submitted rows violating at
372	  least one rule — `results` and `created_at`); rejected or failed
373	  evaluations leave no record, and an empty `rows` submission is recorded
374	  with zero violations. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
375	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
376	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/at?timestamp=...`
377	  — read-only point-in-time single-record look-back, appended one segment
378	  after the evaluation history address and accepting GET only. `timestamp`
379	  must be a timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time (an offset or trailing `Z`);
380	  only evaluation summaries written at or before it form the look-back
381	  window, and the returned summary is the window's highest-sequence record
382	  in exactly the single-record shape of the history (`sequence`, `dataset`,
383	  `version`, `row_count`, `violation_row_count`, `results`, `created_at`).
384	  A window with no recorded evaluation is a normal response, not an error:
385	  the same key set is still returned with `sequence`, `row_count`,
386	  `violation_row_count` and `created_at` set to null (keys are never
387	  omitted) and `results` an empty list. Only persisted evaluation summaries
388	  are read: rules are never re-run, history summaries are never rewritten,
389	  nothing is cached or written, and the window grows naturally as new
390	  evaluations are persisted, so the same data yields the same document byte
391	  for byte across process restarts, and the ordering of rule results never
392	  depends on database natural order. The JSON document is deterministic
393	  (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline). The
394	  path dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body
395	  bytes (whitespace-only included), a missing, repeated, unparseable or
396	  timezone-less `timestamp`, or any other query parameter are a `422` that
397	  writes nothing. Errors keep the stable `{"error", "detail"}` shape without
398	  exposing SQL, stack traces or internal objects; the evaluation history,
399	  the pairwise and point-in-time diffs and every other endpoint are
400	  unchanged.
401	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/diff`
402	  — read-only diff between the two most recent recorded evaluations
403	  (`from_sequence` → `to_sequence`). `added_violation_rows` /
404	  `removed_violation_rows` are the 0-based row indices that started or
405	  stopped violating any rule, and each entry of `rules` carries the rule's
406	  `before`/`after` side (`violation_count` and `violations`), the per-rule
407	  `added_violations` / `removed_violations` and the numeric
408	  `violation_count_delta` (negative, zero or positive). A rule missing from
409	  one side (disabled or created between the two evaluations) has a `null`
410	  side and `null` row-level diff fields. With fewer than two recorded
411	  evaluations the response is an explicit empty result (null sequences,
412	  empty lists), not an error. The path dataset/version resolves first
413	  (`404`); afterwards any request body bytes (whitespace-only included) or
414	  any query parameter are a `422` that writes nothing.
415	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/diff/at?timestamp=...`
416	  — read-only point-in-time companion of the evaluation diff, appended one
417	  segment after the pairwise diff address and accepting GET only.
418	  `timestamp` must be a timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time (an offset or
419	  trailing `Z`); only evaluation summaries written at or before it count as
420	  the look-back window, and the two that participate are the window's
421	  highest-sequence pair — the newest is `to`, its predecessor `from`. The
422	  comparison is exactly the pairwise diff's: `added_violation_rows` /
423	  `removed_violation_rows` are the 0-based row indices that started or
424	  stopped violating any rule, and each `rules` entry carries the rule's
425	  `before`/`after` side (`violation_count` and `violations`), the per-rule
426	  `added_violations` / `removed_violations` and the numeric
427	  `violation_count_delta`. A rule missing from one side (disabled or created
428	  between the two evaluations) has a `null` side and `null` row-level diff
429	  fields — the key is never omitted. A window with fewer than two recorded
430	  evaluations returns the same explicit empty result as the pairwise diff
431	  (null sequences, empty lists), not an error. Only persisted evaluation
432	  summaries are read: rules are never re-run, history summaries are never
433	  rewritten, nothing is cached or written, and the window grows naturally as
434	  new evaluations are persisted, so the same data yields the same document
435	  byte for byte across process restarts. The JSON document is deterministic
436	  (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline). The
437	  path dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body
438	  bytes (whitespace-only included), a missing, repeated, unparseable or
439	  timezone-less `timestamp`, or any other query parameter are a `422` that
440	  writes nothing. Errors keep the stable `{"error", "detail"}` shape without
441	  exposing SQL, stack traces or internal objects; the evaluation history,
442	  the pairwise diff and every other endpoint are unchanged.
443	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/trend`
444	  — read-only trend summary, appended one segment after the evaluation
445	  history address and accepting GET only. The caller sends no request body
446	  and no query parameter. The summary is computed fresh from the persisted
447	  evaluation history on every read: rules are never re-run, history
448	  summaries are never rewritten, nothing is cached or written, and the same
449	  history yields the same document byte for byte across process restarts,
450	  with every ordering explicit rather than dependent on database natural
451	  order.
452	  - `evaluations` lists one entry per evaluation ordered by ascending
453	    `sequence`, each carrying the history summary's `created_at` (write
454	    time), `row_count` (submitted rows) and `violation_row_count`, plus
455	    `violation_row_count_delta` — the change in violation row count against
456	    the previous evaluation; on the first evaluation it is `null` and the
457	    key is never omitted.
458	  - `rules` gives one row per rule that appears in the history, sorted by
459	    rule id ascending, including rules that have since been disabled and
460	    rules that never recorded a violation. Each row carries `rule_id` and
461	    `name`, the cumulative `violation_row_count` (summed over evaluations),
462	    the `violating_evaluation_count`, and `first_violation_sequence` /
463	    `last_violation_sequence` — the sequences of the rule's first and last
464	    violating evaluation, both `null` (never omitted) when the rule never
465	    violated; its counts are zero in that case.
466	  - `totals` reports the whole-version `evaluation_count`, the
467	    `violation_row_count` total (the sum of the per-evaluation counts) and
468	    the `rule_count` of distinct rules the history involves. An empty
469	    history is an explicit empty result (empty `evaluations` and `rules`,
470	    all-zero totals), returned normally rather than as an error.
471	  - The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
472	    whitespace, lowercase booleans, exactly one trailing newline). The path
473	    dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body
474	    bytes (whitespace-only included) or any query parameter are a `422`
475	    that writes nothing. Errors keep the stable `{"error", "detail"}`
476	    shape without exposing SQL, stack traces or internal objects; the
477	    evaluation history, the pairwise and point-in-time diffs, anomaly
478	    detection and every other endpoint are unchanged.

480	### Quality anomaly detection
481	
482	Anomaly detection runs over the persisted evaluation history of a schema
483	version. A version carries at most one detection config; scans append
484	immutable anomaly records that persist across restarts.
485	
486	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
487	  — register the version's detection config. The body contains exactly three
488	  integers: `consecutive_worsening_steps` (at least `2`),
489	  `violation_row_limit` and `rule_violation_limit` (both non-negative).
490	  Returns `201` with the config (`id`, `dataset`, `version`, the three
491	  thresholds, `created_at`). A second config for the same version returns
492	  `409`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing, extra, non-integer or
493	  out-of-range fields → `422` and nothing is written.
494	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
495	  — return the registered config (`404` when none exists). The endpoint takes
496	  no request body and no query parameters (`422`).
497	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/scan`
498	  — run one detection pass over the persisted evaluation history and return
499	  the anomaly records this scan newly added (ordered by `id`); they are
500	  persisted in the same transaction. Scanning without a registered config
501	  returns `409`; an empty history is a successful scan that writes nothing.
502	  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`). Each
503	  record has `id`, `kind`, `sequence` (the history sequence it points to),
504	  `rule_id`, `violation_count` and `created_at`; `kind` is one of:
505	  - `row_limit` — the evaluation's `violation_row_count` exceeds
506	    `violation_row_limit` (`rule_id` is `null`).
507	  - `rule_limit` — one rule's violation count in the evaluation exceeds
508	    `rule_violation_limit`; `rule_id` carries the rule's id.
509	  - `trend` — the violation row counts of adjacent evaluations strictly
510	    increase and the consecutive increase count at the tail of the history
511	    reaches `consecutive_worsening_steps`; the record points to the final
512	    evaluation of the increasing sequence (`rule_id` is `null`). A shorter
513	    run or any decline produces no trend record.
514	
515	  A record with the same kind, history sequence and rule id is never
516	  duplicated: repeated scans only persist and return newly appearing
517	  anomalies, and concurrent scans store each anomaly exactly once with
518	  contiguous ids.
519	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/anomalies`
520	  — list every anomaly record of the version sorted by `id` ascending (empty
521	  when there are none, never an error). Same `404`/`422` rules as the scan
522	  endpoint; nothing is written.
523	
524	### Quality gate
525	
526	The quality gate is the release-readiness verdict of a schema version. It is
527	computed fresh from the persisted records on every read — nothing is cached,
528	re-run or written, and the rule definitions are never consulted (violations
529	recorded for rules since disabled still count).
530	
531	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate` — return the
532	  verdict as a deterministic JSON document (fixed key order, compact
533	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
534	  `{"dataset", "version", "verdict", "reasons", "counts"}`.
535	  - `verdict` is one of:
536	    - `pass` — the latest recorded evaluation passed every rule and no
537	      anomaly record exists; a zero-violation evaluation left by an empty
538	      `rows` submission is a valid basis.
539	    - `undetermined` — no evaluation was ever recorded; `reasons` is empty
540	      and the read succeeds (never an error).
541	    - `fail` — the latest recorded evaluation still has violating rows, or
542	      the version carries any anomaly record.
543	  - `reasons` lists every factor that lowers the verdict, sorted by `kind`,
544	    `sequence` and `rule_id` (null ids first), all ascending. Each reason has
545	    `kind`, `sequence`, `rule_id` and `violation_count` (a missing rule id is
546	    `null`, never omitted). Every rule with violations in the latest
547	    evaluation contributes one `violation` reason with its violation row
548	    count; every persisted anomaly record contributes one reason of its own
549	    kind (`row_limit`, `rule_limit` or `trend`). A rule that appears in both
550	    yields two reasons — they are never merged or deduplicated.
551	  - `counts` reports how many persisted records the verdict examined:
552	    `evaluations`, `anomalies` and `reasons` (the length of the reason list).
553	  - The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters: any body
554	    bytes — including whitespace-only ones — or any query parameter are a
555	    `422`, checked after the path dataset/version resolves (`404` first).
556	    Nothing is written on any rejection.
557	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate/at?timestamp=...`
558	  — the same verdict as it stood at a requested instant. `timestamp` must be
559	  a timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time; only evaluations and anomaly records
560	  written at or before it count, and the latest evaluation of that window is
561	  the one with the highest sequence inside it. The response is the same
562	  deterministic document as the bare gate (`dataset`, `version`, `verdict`,
563	  `reasons`, `counts`, one trailing newline), with the counts covering only
564	  the records inside the window. A window without any evaluation is
565	  `undetermined` with an empty reason list — a normal response, never an
566	  error. The endpoint accepts GET only and is strictly read-only. The path
567	  dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body bytes
568	  (whitespace-only included), a missing, repeated, unparseable or
569	  timezone-less `timestamp`, or any other query parameter are a `422` that
570	  writes nothing.
571	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/quality-gate-export` — read-only cross-version
572	  export of the dataset's whole quality gate state, computed fresh on every
573	  read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or deleted, and no
574	  evaluation, anomaly record or gate verdict is touched). The path carries
575	  only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no query parameters —
576	  any body bytes, including a purely whitespace or single-space body, or any
577	  query parameter → `422`; an unknown dataset → `404`, checked before the
578	  request shape, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the compliance
579	  exports. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an empty
580	  `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON document is
581	  deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
582	  newline):
583	
584	  ```json
585	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"verdict":"fail","reason_count":1,"violation_row_count":2},{"version":2,"verdict":"undetermined","reason_count":0,"violation_row_count":null}],"totals":{"version_count":2,"failed_count":1,"reason_count":1,"violation_row_count":2}}
586	  ```
587	
588	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
589	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry has
590	  exactly `version`, `verdict`, `reason_count` and `violation_row_count` in
591	  that order. `verdict` is the current per-version gate verdict (one of
592	  `pass`, `undetermined`, `fail`) under exactly the same computation as the
593	  per-version gate read; `reason_count` is the number of reasons currently
594	  lowering that verdict (the length of the per-version gate's reason list);
595	  `violation_row_count` is the violation row count of the latest recorded
596	  evaluation and is `null` — never omitted — when the version was never
597	  evaluated. `totals` has exactly `version_count`, `failed_count`,
598	  `reason_count` and `violation_row_count`: the number of version entries,
599	  the number of versions whose verdict is `fail`, and the sums of the
600	  per-version reason and violation row counts (null violation row counts
601	  count as zero).
602	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/quality-rule-coverage` — read-only cross-version
603	  check of how the dataset's schema fields are covered by quality rules,
604	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or
605	  deleted, and no rule definition or evaluation record is touched). The path
606	  carries only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no query
607	  parameters — any body bytes, including a purely whitespace or single-space
608	  body, or any query parameter → `422`; an unknown dataset → `404`, checked
609	  before the request shape, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
610	  compliance exports. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an
611	  empty `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
612	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
613	  trailing newline; the same data renders byte-identically after a process
614	  restart and ordering never depends on the database's natural order):
615	
616	  ```json
617	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"fields":[{"field":"amount","coverage":"disabled","kinds":["numeric_range"],"rule_ids":[3]},{"field":"id","coverage":"enabled","kinds":["not_null","unique"],"rule_ids":[1,2]},{"field":"region","coverage":"unregistered","kinds":null,"rule_ids":null}]}],"totals":{"version_count":1,"field_count":3,"enabled_count":1,"disabled_count":1,"unregistered_count":1}}
618	  ```
619	
620	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
621	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry has
622	  exactly `version` and `fields`, with every field of the version listed by
623	  field name ascending. Each field entry has exactly `field`, `coverage`,
624	  `kinds` and `rule_ids` in that order. `coverage` is one of the literals
625	  `enabled` (at least one enabled rule references the field), `disabled`
626	  (rules reference the field but all of them are disabled) and
627	  `unregistered` (no rule references the field). `kinds` is the
628	  de-duplicated list of referencing rule kinds sorted by literal value and
629	  `rule_ids` the referencing rules' ids de-duplicated and sorted ascending;
630	  every field of a unique rule counts as referenced. When a field is also
631	  referenced by disabled rules alongside enabled ones, their kinds and ids
632	  are included too. For an `unregistered` field both `kinds` and `rule_ids`
633	  are `null` — the keys are never omitted. `totals` has exactly
634	  `version_count`, `field_count`, `enabled_count`, `disabled_count` and
635	  `unregistered_count`: each is the sum of the per-version entries, and the
636	  field count equals the sum of the three per-state counts.

638	### Privacy policies
639	
640	Privacy policies attach a sensitivity classification and masking strategy to a
641	single field of a schema version, enabling role-based de-identification of row
642	data. Policies (including their enabled state) are persisted across restarts.
643	
644	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — register a
645	  policy. Body:
646	  `{"field": "email", "classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles": ["analyst"]}`.
647	  `field` must name an existing field of the version; `classification` is a
648	  non-empty string; `masking` is `redact` or `partial`; `allowed_roles` is an
649	  array of distinct, non-empty role names and may be empty. Returns `201` with
650	  the submitted fields plus `id`, `enabled` (defaults to `true`) and
651	  `created_at`. Registering two policies for the same field within one version
652	  returns `409`. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; other invalid input →
653	  `422` and nothing is written.
654	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — list policies
655	  sorted by `id` ascending.
656	- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
657	  enable or disable a policy. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
658	  the updated policy. Unknown policy/dataset/version → `404`.
659	- `PUT /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
660	  revise a policy. Body carries exactly the three adjustable fields:
661	  `{"classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles":
662	  ["analyst"]}`, using the same value rules as registration — a non-empty
663	  `classification` after trimming, `masking` of `redact` or `partial`, and an
664	  `allowed_roles` array of distinct, non-empty-after-trimming role names that
665	  may be empty. The three fields are replaced together from one whole
666	  submission. The revision never changes the policy id, the field it belongs
667	  to, its `enabled` state or its `created_at`; it writes only the policy
668	  itself — no policy is created, no identification record is touched and no
669	  masking suggestion is registered. Returns `200` with the updated policy in
670	  the same shape as the policy read, and the revision survives restarts. The
671	  next privacy view read (and every later masked read) judges each value by
672	  the revised classification, masking and allowed roles. Already-written
673	  masking-hit records, access records and cleanup requests are unaffected —
674	  their contents and ordering stay as written; the grouping of the summary,
675	  diff and reconciliation responses keeps the same counting rules, while the
676	  policy classification and masking reported on trend rows (and the policy
677	  entries of the coverage check and compliance export) reflect the current
678	  values. Advisory masking suggestions are unaffected. Unknown
679	  dataset/version/policy → `404`, judged before every request-shape check;
680	  missing or extra fields, a blank `classification`, an illegal `masking`
681	  value, duplicate or blank `allowed_roles` entries, an empty or
682	  whitespace-only body, malformed JSON, a non-object payload or any query
683	  parameter → `422` and nothing is written. Concurrent revisions of the same
684	  policy have exactly one winner; the loser receives `409` and changes no
685	  field.
686	
687	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view` — return a
688	  role-scoped, order-preserving copy of submitted rows. Body:
689	  `{"role": "guest", "rows": [{...}, ...]}` with a non-empty `role` and a list
690	  of row objects. Response: `{"dataset", "version", "rows"}`. Only enabled
691	  policies whose field appears in a row mask the value when `role` is not in
692	  `allowed_roles`:
693	  - `redact` replaces every non-`null` value with `"***"`.
694	  - `partial` keeps the first character and last two characters of strings
695	    longer than 4 characters (e.g. `"alice@example.com"` → `"aom"`); every other
696	    non-`null` value (short strings, numbers, booleans, …) is replaced with
697	    `"***"`.
698	  - `null` values and fields without a policy are returned unchanged; rows
699	    missing a covered field are left without it.
700	
701	  Every successful view also appends one audit record per value it actually
702	  masked (the same field masked in several rows yields one record per masked
703	  value; a role in `allowed_roles`, a `null` value, an uncovered field or a
704	  disabled policy never hits); the records are persisted per version and are
705	  append-only.
706	
707	  Every successful view additionally appends exactly one access record,
708	  whether or not it masked any value (an empty `rows` submission is recorded
709	  too). Rejected or failed views leave neither kind of record.
710	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/access-records`
711	  — list every access record of the version, ordered by `sequence` ascending
712	  (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has `sequence`,
713	  `role`, `row_count` (the number of submitted rows), `masked_count` (the
714	  number of masking-hit records the same view wrote, so the two logs
715	  cross-check) and `created_at`. The endpoint takes no request body and no
716	  query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is
717	  written.
718	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records`
719	  — list every masking-hit record of the version, ordered by `sequence`
720	  ascending (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has
721	  `sequence`, `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking` and `created_at`. The
722	  endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown
723	  dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is written.
724	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/search`
725	  — read-only filtered retrieval of the same masking-hit records. The
726	  response is the same record collection as the full list (each record has
727	  `sequence`, `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking` and `created_at`),
728	  sorted by `sequence` ascending; a filter that matches nothing returns an
729	  empty array, never an error. All filters are optional query parameters and
730	  combine with AND:
731	  - `role` — exact match against the requesting role recorded on the hit,
732	    case-insensitive (no substring or other fuzzy matching).
733	  - `field` — exact match against the hit field name, case-insensitive.
734	  - `start` / `end` — closed write-time interval: a record matches when its
735	    `created_at` is between the bounds inclusive. Each bound is a
736	    timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time (offset or `Z`); either bound may be
737	    given alone. `start` later than `end` → `422`.
738	
739	  The endpoint takes no request body; an unparseable or timezone-less
740	  `start`/`end`, or any query parameter other than `role`, `field`, `start`
741	  and `end`, → `422`. Unknown dataset/version → `404`, with the same
742	  404-before-422 precedence as the record list. It is strictly read-only:
743	  no record is written, modified or deleted and the summary/diff responses
744	  are unaffected.
745	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/summary`
746	  — read-only compliance summary computed fresh from the persisted records on
747	  every read (no caching, nothing is written or deleted). Response:
748	  `{"dataset", "version", "groups"}`; `groups` is an empty array when the
749	  version has no records. Each group merges records with the same `field`,
750	  `policy_id`, `role` and `masking` (different roles or masking modes stay
751	  separate) and lists `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking`, `hit_count`
752	  (one record counts as one hit), `first_hit_at` and `last_hit_at` (the
753	  earliest and latest record `created_at` in the group). Groups sort by
754	  `field`, then `policy_id`, `role` and `masking`, all ascending. The
755	  endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown
756	  dataset/version → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
757	  record list.
758	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/trend`
759	  — read-only hit trend aggregated by privacy policy, computed fresh from the
760	  persisted records on every read (no caching, nothing is written or deleted).
761	  Hits of the same policy merge across roles (a disabled policy's historical
762	  hits still count). Response: `{"dataset", "version", "policies", "totals"}`;
763	  `policies` is an empty array when the version has no records. Each policy
764	  row carries `policy_id`, `field`, `classification`, `masking`, `total_hits`
765	  and `days`; policies sort by `policy_id` ascending. `days` lists only UTC
766	  calendar days with hits (a write time with a non-zero offset buckets by its
767	  UTC day), sorted ascending with no zero-filled gaps; each entry has `day`
768	  (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `hit_count` (one record counts once), `hit_count_delta`
769	  (difference from the previous listed day, `null` on the first) and `trend`
770	  (`up`/`down`/`flat`, or `none` on the first day). `totals` gives
771	  `total_hits` (the sum of the row totals), `policy_count` (policies with
772	  hits) and `day_count` (distinct hit days over the whole version, the
773	  per-policy day union). The endpoint takes no request body and no query
774	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`, with the same
775	  404-before-422 precedence as the record list.
776	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests`
777	  — open a two-stage retention cleanup request for the version's masking-hit
778	  records. Body contains exactly `reason` and `before`:
779	  `{"reason": "legal hold expired", "before": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`.
780	  `reason` must be a string that is non-empty after trimming whitespace;
781	  `before` must be an ISO-8601 date-time carrying a timezone (offset or `Z`),
782	  and a record belongs to the target set only when its hit write time is
783	  strictly earlier than that instant. Creating a request only returns a
784	  preview — no hit record is deleted or modified, and the record list,
785	  search, summary, diff, reconcile and trend responses stay unchanged.
786	  Returns `201` with `id`, `reason` (trimmed), `before` (echoed as
787	  submitted), `status` (`pending`), `created_at` and a `preview` block:
788	  `hit_count` (the number of records that would be cleaned up),
789	  `first_hit_at` / `last_hit_at` (the earliest and latest hit times in the
790	  target set, `null` when the set is empty) and `fields` (the distinct field
791	  names involved, sorted ascending; `[]` when empty). The target set is
792	  fixed at creation time: masking-hit records written afterwards never enter
793	  the request even when they precede the cutoff by clock time. At most one
794	  pending request may exist per version; creating another while one is open
795	  returns `409` and writes nothing (confirmed requests never block a new
796	  one). Unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing/non-string/blank `reason`,
797	  missing/unparseable/timezone-less `before`, an extra body field, a
798	  non-JSON/non-object body or any query parameter → `422` and nothing is
799	  written, with 404 taking precedence.
800	- `GET .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests` — list the
801	  version's cleanup requests sorted by request `id` ascending (empty when
802	  there are none). Confirmed requests stay listed and requests survive
803	  process restarts. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
804	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
805	- `POST .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests/{request_id}/confirm`
806	  — confirm a request with an empty request body and no query parameters.
807	  Confirmation atomically deletes exactly the target set frozen at creation
808	  and sets `status` to `confirmed`; the response is the request plus
809	  `confirmed_at` and `deleted_count` (the number of records actually
810	  deleted, possibly zero). Confirming an already-confirmed request returns
811	  `409` and never changes data again; concurrent confirmations have exactly
812	  one winner (the others get `409`) and can never leave the records half
813	  deleted. After a cleanup the surviving hit records keep their original
814	  `sequence` numbers and later hits continue the existing increasing run
815	  without reusing cleaned numbers; the record list and search return only
816	  surviving records, and summary, trend, diff and reconcile recompute from
817	  them. Access records are not cleaned up and the processing-task audit
818	  chain remains immutable. A request body or query parameter on the confirm
819	  endpoint → `422`; unknown dataset/version/request → `404` (precedence
820	  matches the hit-record reads), and confirming a confirmed request →
821	  `409`.
822	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-compliance-export` — read-only
823	  cross-version export of the dataset's whole privacy compliance state,
824	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or
825	  deleted, and no hit record, access record or cleanup request is touched).
826	  The path carries only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no
827	  query parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, with the same
828	  404-before-422 precedence as the hit-record reads. A dataset without
829	  schema versions returns `200` with an empty `versions` array and all-zero
830	  totals, never an error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
831	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
832	
833	  ```json
834	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"policies":[...],"hit_count":0,"masked_count":1,"view_count":2,"cleanup_requests":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
835	  ```
836	
837	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
838	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
839	  has exactly `version`, `policies`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
840	  `view_count`, `cleanup_requests` in that order. `policies` lists the
841	  version's registered policies ordered by policy id; each policy has `id`,
842	  `field`, `classification`, `masking`, `allowed_roles` and `enabled`.
843	  `cleanup_requests` lists the version's cleanup requests ordered by request
844	  id (both pending and confirmed are retained); each has `id`, `reason`,
845	  `status` and `created_at`. `hit_count` is the number of masking-hit
846	  records currently stored for the version, `masked_count` is the sum of the
847	  access records' masked-value counts and `view_count` is the number of
848	  access records; all three reflect the records surviving a confirmed
849	  cleanup. `totals` has exactly `policy_count`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
850	  `view_count` and `cleanup_request_count`, each the sum of the per-version
851	  values over the whole dataset.
852	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-policy-coverage` — read-only cross-version
853	  check of the dataset's privacy policy coverage, computed fresh on every
854	  read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or deleted, and no policy
855	  or identification record is touched). The path carries only the dataset
856	  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an
857	  unknown dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
858	  compliance export. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an
859	  empty `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
860	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly
861	  one trailing newline):
862	
863	  ```json
864	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"fields":[...],"candidates":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
865	  ```
866	
867	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
868	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
869	  has exactly `version`, `fields`, `candidates` in that order. `fields`
870	  lists every field of the version ordered by field name; each entry has
871	  `field`, `coverage`, `classification`, `masking` and `enabled`, where
872	  `coverage` is `enabled` (an enabled policy is registered), `disabled` (a
873	  policy is registered but disabled) or `unregistered` (no policy), and the
874	  last three keys report the registered policy's classification, masking and
875	  enabled state (all `null` when no policy is registered). `candidates`
876	  lists the advisory suggestions for fields that were identified with at
877	  least one name or sample hit but carry no privacy policy yet, ordered by
878	  identification record id ascending; each candidate has exactly `field`,
879	  `classification` and `masking`, and an identified field whose name and
880	  samples both missed does not appear. The candidates are a compliance
881	  self-check reference only: they never register a policy and never rewrite
882	  an identification record. `totals` has exactly `version_count`,
883	  `field_count`, `enabled_count`, `disabled_count`, `unregistered_count`
884	  and `candidate_count`, each the sum of the per-version values over the
885	  whole dataset.
886	
887	### Sensitive-field identification
888	
889	Sensitive-field identification produces candidate annotations for the fields of
890	a schema version. It complements the manual privacy policies but never creates
891	or modifies one: an identification is advisory only. Records (including their
892	stable ids) persist across restarts.
893	
894	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
895	  identify one field. The body contains exactly `field` and `samples`:
896	  `{"field": "contact_email", "samples": ["alice@example.com"]}`. `field` must
897	  name an existing field of the version; its name and type are taken from the
898	  version definition. `samples` is an array of JSON scalars (strings, numbers,
899	  booleans or `null`) and may be empty; objects or arrays reject the whole
900	  request. The samples are never stored or echoed back. Returns the record;
901	  the first submission for a field returns `201`, re-running the same field
902	  refreshes the record in place (the id is unchanged) and returns `200`.
903	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
904	  return every identification record of the version sorted by id ascending
905	  (empty when there are none). The endpoint takes no request body and no query
906	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
907	
908	  Each record has `id`, `field`, `field_type`, `evidence`, `confidence`,
909	  `source` and `created_at`. `source` references the identified field as
910	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. `evidence` is the ordered, de-duplicated
911	  list of hit kinds, name hits before sample hits:
912	
913	  - **Name hits** — the field name contains a sensitive word case-insensitively
914	    as a substring. The words are `email`, `phone`, `id_card`, `password`,
915	    `token` and `birth`, emitting `name:<word>` in that order.
916	  - **Sample hits** — only string sample values are inspected (numbers,
917	    booleans and `null` never hit), and only when the field's declared type is
918	    `string`; a field declared with any other type is matched by name alone,
919	    even when a sample looks like an email. `sample:email` requires exactly
920	    one `@` with non-empty text on both sides and a dot in the domain;
921	    `sample:phone` requires an 11-digit string starting with `1`. Either format
922	    matching is sufficient.
923	
924	  `confidence` is `high` when both the name and the samples hit, `medium` for
925	  samples only, `low` for the name only and `none` when neither side hits
926	  (`evidence` is then an empty list but the record is still generated).
927	
928	  One record is kept per field: a re-run overwrites the evidence and confidence
929	  in place with a stable id. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; a field that does
930	  not exist in the version → `404`; missing or extra body fields, a
931	  non-string or blank field name, a `samples` value that is not an array of
932	  scalars (objects and arrays included), an empty body, malformed JSON or any
933	  query parameter → `422` and nothing is written.
934	
935	#### Masking strategy suggestions
936	
937	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions`
938	  — read-only advisory masking-strategy candidates derived from the version's
939	  identification records. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
940	  parameters (`422` if either is present, with nothing written); unknown
941	  dataset/version → `404`. A version without identification records returns an
942	  empty list rather than an error.
943	
944	  Each candidate has exactly `field`, `classification`, `masking` and
945	  `allowed_roles`. Only records whose name or samples hit produce a candidate;
946	  a record with empty evidence is omitted. Candidates follow the identification
947	  records' `id` ascending and are recomputed on every read, so refreshing an
948	  identification changes the suggestion on the next request. The endpoint
949	  writes nothing, never registers a privacy policy and leaves the
950	  identification records' fields, ordering and refresh semantics untouched;
951	  the privacy view continues to mask according to registered policies only.
952	
953	  - `classification` is `PII` for email, phone, id-card and birthday hits, and
954	    `CREDENTIAL` for password and token hits. A field hitting both is `PII`.
955	  - `masking` reuses the privacy-view vocabulary: `partial` for `PII`
956	    candidates and `redact` for `CREDENTIAL` candidates (a both-kinds field
957	    takes `partial`); no new masking format is introduced.
958	  - `allowed_roles` is always an empty list: the suggested masking applies to
959	    every role, granting none an unmasked view.
960	
961	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions/register`
962	  — turn the current advisory candidates into registered privacy policies. The
963	  body contains only `{"fields": ["<field>", ...]}`: a non-empty array of
964	  distinct field names, each non-empty after trimming and naming an existing
965	  field of the version that currently has a masking suggestion candidate.
966	  Returns `201` with one privacy policy record per requested field, in the
967	  request's field-name order; each record has the same fields as the manual
968	  policy creation response (`id`, `field`, `classification`, `masking`,
969	  `allowed_roles`, `enabled`, `created_at`), is enabled by default and gets a
970	  service-generated id and timestamp. Each policy copies its candidate's
971	  `classification` and `masking` verbatim with the candidate's empty
972	  `allowed_roles`, so after registration every role sees those fields masked;
973	  the next privacy view read masks according to the new policies. The whole
974	  batch is validated before anything is written, so any rejection writes no
975	  policy and no timestamp. Unknown dataset/version, or a named field that does
976	  not exist in the version → `404`; a field without an available candidate
977	  (never identified, or whose identification record currently yields no
978	  candidate) or one that already has a privacy policy → `409`; two concurrent
979	  registrations of the same field leave exactly one winner. Missing or extra
980	  body fields, an empty `fields` array, duplicate, non-string or blank names,
981	  an empty body, a whitespace-only body, malformed JSON or any query parameter
982	  → `422` and nothing is written. Registration only reads the identification
983	  records and field definitions; it never writes or auto-refreshes an
984	  identification, and the read-only suggestions endpoint stays unchanged.
985	
986	### Row snapshots
987	
988	A row snapshot persistently records the rows of a schema version at one point in
989	time. Snapshots (including their rows) survive restarts.
990	
991	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — persist a snapshot.
992	  Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}` where `rows` must be an array of JSON objects
993	  (it may be empty). The JSON values and the order of rows/object keys are deep
994	  copied verbatim. A SHA-256 content fingerprint of the saved row sequence is
995	  computed at creation and written together with the rows in one atomic write,
996	  so it can later attest that the persisted rows are unchanged; the fingerprint
997	  is not part of the response, which stays `id`, `dataset`, `version`,
998	  `created_at` and `row_count` (no rows). In the same transaction the service
999	  also maintains the snapshot diff cache incrementally (see "Snapshot diff
1000	  cache" below): the canonical form of every row (key-sorted compact JSON text
1001	  in stored row order) and the sorted set of top-level field names are written
1002	  together with the snapshot, and one `created` record is appended to the
1003	  version's cache trail. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; malformed or
1004	  non-object rows → `422` and nothing is written.
1005	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — list snapshot
1006	  metadata sorted by `id` ascending (no `rows`).
1007	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}` — return
1008	  the metadata together with the saved `rows`. Unknown dataset/version/snapshot
1009	  → `404`.
1010	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/verify` —
1011	  read-only content-fingerprint verification, appended one segment after the
1012	  single-snapshot read address and accepting GET only. On every read the
1013	  fingerprint of the currently persisted row sequence is recomputed and
1014	  compared with the fingerprint stored with the snapshot at creation; the
1015	  snapshot and its rows are only read, never written or modified. The JSON
1016	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, lowercase
1017	  booleans, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
1018	  `version`, `snapshot_id`, `row_count`, `stored_hash`, `computed_hash` and
1019	  `valid` in that order. `stored_hash` is the fingerprint written at creation,
1020	  `computed_hash` the freshly recomputed one and `valid` is `true` exactly
1021	  while both agree; directly changing, adding, deleting or replacing a saved
1022	  row makes them differ and changes `computed_hash`. Both verdicts return
1023	  `200`. The fingerprint hashes the saved row sequence as a JSON array in row
1024	  order with each object's keys sorted by Unicode code point, compact text,
1025	  non-ASCII characters unescaped, UTF-8 encoded and SHA-256 digested to
1026	  hexadecimal; array order and value types are significant (integers, floats,
1027	  strings and booleans never compare equal and negative zero is represented
1028	  distinctly), an empty snapshot is fingerprinted normally and the same rows
1029	  yield the same digest across restarts. The verification reads only the
1030	  snapshot and its rows — no lineage, quality, privacy or task state — and
1031	  does not affect retention or deletion; a confirmed-deleted snapshot is no
1032	  longer addressable here either (`404`). The endpoint takes no request body
1033	  and no query parameters: any body bytes — including whitespace-only ones —
1034	  or any query parameter are a `422`, checked after the path
1035	  dataset/version/snapshot resolves, so an unknown dataset, version or
1036	  snapshot is a `404` first. Every rejection writes nothing.
1037	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at?timestamp=<ISO-8601>` —
1038	  return the most recent snapshot whose `created_at` is not later than
1039	  `timestamp`, including its rows. The timestamp must be a timezone-aware
1040	  ISO-8601 date-time (an offset or trailing `Z`): missing, invalid or
1041	  timezone-less values return `422`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; when no
1042	  snapshot exists at or before the timestamp the response is `404`.
1043	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/diff?from=<ISO-8601>&to=<ISO-8601>`
1044	  — read-only time-travel row diff, appended one segment after the bare-row
1045	  time lookup and accepting GET only. Each of `from` (the baseline) and `to`
1046	  (the target) must be a timezone-aware ISO-8601 date-time; each side
1047	  independently selects the latest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later
1048	  than its own timestamp (the same selection as the bare-row lookup), so the
1049	  two times may resolve to the same snapshot and a `to` earlier than `from` is
1050	  valid — the two snapshots are simply compared in their named order. The
1051	  comparison reads snapshots and rows and writes nothing. The JSON document
1052	  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
1053	  newline) with top-level keys `from_timestamp`, `to_timestamp`,
1054	  `from_snapshot_id`, `to_snapshot_id`, `added`, `removed`, `fields_added`
